=== PMID: 25441702 ===

Title: A systematic review identifies valid comorbidity indices derived from administrative health data.

Journal/Date: Journal of clinical epidemiology (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Comorbidity, Forecasting, Hospital Mortality, Hospitalization, Humans, Medical Records, Reproducibility of Results, Vital Statistics


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVES]: To conduct a systematic review of studies reporting on the development or validation of comorbidity indices using administrative health data and compare their ability to predict outcomes related to comorbidity (ie, construct validity).
[STUDY DESIGN AND SETTING]: We conducted a comprehensive literature search of MEDLINE and EMBASE, until September 2012. After title and abstract screen, relevant articles were selected for review by two independent investigators. Predictive validity and model fit were measured using c-statistic for dichotomous outcomes and R(2) for continuous outcomes.
[RESULTS]: Our review includes 76 articles. Two categories of comorbidity indices were identified: those identifying comorbidities based on diagnoses, using International Classification of Disease codes from hospitalization or outpatient data, and based on medications, using pharmacy data. The ability of indices studied to predict morbidity-related outcomes ranged from poor (C statistic ≤ 0.69) to excellent (C statistic >0.80) depending on the specific index, outcome measured, and study population. Diagnosis-based measures, particularly the Elixhauser Index and the Romano adaptation of the Charlson Index, resulted in higher ability to predict mortality outcomes. Medication-based indices, such as the Chronic Disease Score, demonstrated better performance for predicting health care utilization.
[CONCLUSION]: A number of valid comorbidity indices derived from administrative data are available. Selection of an appropriate index should take into account the type of data available, study population, and specific outcome of interest.

[BACKGROUND]: Maternal critical illness occurs in 1.2 to 4.7 of every 1000 live births in the United States and approximately 1 in 100 women who become critically ill will die. Patient characteristics and comorbid conditions are commonly summarized as an index or score for the purpose of predicting the likelihood of dying; however, most such indices have arisen from non-pregnant patient populations. We sought to systematically review comorbidity indices used in health administrative datasets of pregnant women, in order to critically appraise their measurement properties and recommend optimal tools for clinicians and maternal health researchers.
[METHODS]: We conducted a systematic search of MEDLINE and EMBASE to identify studies published from 1946 and 1947, respectively, to May 2017 that describe predictive validity of comorbidity indices using health administrative datasets in the field of maternal health research. Evolution of this and other tools for risk prediction and risk adjustment in pregnant and post-partum patients is an important area for ongoing study.

key_findings.finding: Yes—one directly relevant systematic review (76 articles; MEDLINE/EMBASE through September 2012) concluded that multiple comorbidity indices derived from administrative data are valid, but predictive validity was outcome- and population-dependent: c-statistics ranged from poor (≤0.69) to excellent (>0.80). Diagnosis-based Elixhauser and Romano-adapted Charlson performed better for mortality, whereas medication-based indices such as the Chronic Disease Score performed better for healthcare utilization. The review recommends choosing the index according to available data, population, and outcome rather than treating one index as universally best.

A systematic review focused on orthopedic populations (16 administrative-data cohort studies) found AUCs from poor to excellent. For in-hospital mortality, Elixhauser AUCs were 0.70–0.92 and Charlson AUCs 0.68–0.89; for 1-year mortality, pooled/overall ranges were 0.67–0.77 for Elixhauser and 0.69–0.77 for Charlson. It concluded that ECI and CCI could be used equally for mortality adjustment in orthopedic settings, while performance was lower for other time horizons.

The maternal-health systematic review found only two eligible studies covering three administrative-data indices (Maternal Comorbidity Index, Charlson, and Elixhauser). Only the Maternal Comorbidity Index was derived and validated specifically in pregnant/postpartum women; its mortality c-statistic was 0.675, indicating modest discrimination. The review noted marginal sensibility across indices and insufficient evidence for reliability across datasets, so general-population CCI/ECI validity should not be assumed in pregnancy.

source_tools.relevance: Direct systematic-review population-specific findings and limitations

key_findings.finding: Key included/related validation studies support transportable but context-specific validity: Quan et al. developed ICD-9/ICD-10 coding algorithms for Charlson and Elixhauser in Canadian hospital discharge data; Southern et al. compared both measures in disease-specific cohorts and reported ICD-9 versus ICD-10 c-statistic differences of 0–0.04, with performance varying by cohort; van Walraven et al. derived and internally validated a point-based Elixhauser score in 345,795 Ottawa hospitalizations; and Johns Hopkins ADGs were derived/validated in 10,498,413 Ontario ambulatory adults for 1-year mortality. These are validation populations for hospital or ambulatory administrative data, not evidence of universal validity across settings or outcomes.

source_tools.relevance: Elixhauser derivation/validation and Johns Hopkins ADG validation study

key_findings.finding: For Johns Hopkins ACG specifically, the search identified validation and risk-stratification evidence but not a dedicated systematic review establishing it as a universally valid comorbidity index. A systematic review of primary-care risk-stratification tools describes ACG as predicting utilization costs, hospitalization, and emergency visits; the underlying ADG validation study evaluated 1-year mortality in a very large Ontario ambulatory population. Thus, ACG/ADG is supported as a validated administrative risk-adjustment/case-mix approach for selected outcomes and populations, but evidence is less directly comparable to the CCI/ECI systematic-review evidence.
